Task complexity.var_definition: breadth, interdependence, and ambiguity of the assigned product work

var_value_description.low complexity: single feature with clear requirements and few dependencies
var_value_description.medium complexity: multiple related features with some cross-team dependencies
var_value_description.high complexity: multi-component initiative with high ambiguity and many dependencies

Deadline pressure.var_definition: tightness of the mandated delivery timeline for the product work

var_value_description.relaxed deadline: ample time relative to scope with schedule slack
var_value_description.standard deadline: typical timeline with moderate schedule pressure
var_value_description.tight deadline: aggressive timeline with little or no schedule slack

Decision authority.var_definition: extent to which the subject_agent is formally empowered to make binding product decisions

var_value_description.no authority: can analyze and recommend but cannot make binding decisions
var_value_description.shared authority: co-decides with at least one other role for major choices
var_value_description.full authority: can make final product decisions within the project scope

Process rigidity.var_definition: strictness of formal procedures governing how the subject_agent may pursue product work

var_value_description.high flexibility: may bypass or adapt formal steps with minimal justification
var_value_description.standard rules: expected to follow standard process with occasional exceptions
var_value_description.strict compliance: must follow prescribed stages and approvals with no deviations

Market volatility.var_definition: frequency and magnitude of external market changes affecting product requirements

var_value_description.stable market: customer needs and competitor offerings change slowly and predictably
var_value_description.moderate volatility: periodic shifts in priorities or competitive moves
var_value_description.high volatility: frequent disruptive changes in customer needs or competition

Information availability.var_definition: amount and quality of accessible data, documentation, and prior research

var_value_description.sparse information: few relevant documents or data points with major gaps
var_value_description.partial information: some key documents and data but with notable uncertainties
var_value_description.rich information: comprehensive, up-to-date data and documentation coverage

Capacity slack.var_definition: degree of available engineering and design capacity for the initiative

var_value_description.overloaded team: teams are overcommitted with little room for new work
var_value_description.balanced load: teams are near full utilization but can absorb some work
var_value_description.slack capacity: teams have notable unused capacity for additional tasks

Stakeholder alignment.var_definition: baseline agreement among cross-functional stakeholders about product goals and priorities

var_value_description.high conflict: stakeholders hold divergent goals and frequently disagree on direction
var_value_description.mixed alignment: stakeholders share some goals but differ on key priorities
var_value_description.strong alignment: stakeholders broadly agree on goals, priorities, and success criteria

Response speed.var_definition: typical promptness of other actors in replying to requests and providing inputs

var_value_description.slow responses: stakeholders often delay replies beyond the current round or day
var_value_description.average speed: stakeholders usually respond within the expected time window
var_value_description.rapid responses: stakeholders respond quickly and proactively to requests

Outcome stakes.var_definition: severity of positive and negative consequences tied to success or failure of product decisions

var_value_description.low stakes: outcomes have limited business or career impact and reversible effects
var_value_description.moderate stakes: outcomes materially affect team metrics but are partly recoverable
var_value_description.high stakes: outcomes strongly affect business results, reputation, or careers

covariance_structure.Task complexity AND Role interdependence: More complex initiatives span more components and teams, so higher task complexity generally implies higher role interdependence.
covariance_structure.Task complexity AND Market volatility: In more volatile markets, product work is more often framed as broad, multi-component initiatives, increasing typical task complexity.
covariance_structure.Task complexity AND Information availabi: When tasks are complex and markets are volatile, information is usually only partially available because conditions change faster than documentation can be updated.
covariance_structure.Deadline pressure AND Capacity slack: Overloaded teams are more likely to face tight deadlines, while slack capacity usually goes with relaxed or standard timelines.
covariance_structure.Capacity slack AND Response speed: Teams with slack capacity can respond to requests faster, whereas overloaded teams more often exhibit slow or merely average response times.
covariance_structure.Outcome stakes AND Process rigidity: Higher stakes (e.g., regulatory, safety, major revenue) tend to drive stricter, more formalized processes, while low stakes allow more flexible processes.
covariance_structure.Outcome stakes AND Market volatility: In volatile markets, product bets more often have material business impact, so higher market volatility tends to coincide with higher outcome stakes.
covariance_structure.Stakeholder alignment AND Decision autho: When stakeholders are strongly aligned, organizations more often grant clear (sometimes full) decision authority to a lead; when conflict is high, authority is more often shared or diffused.

potential_interactions.Task complexity: As task complexity increases, higher role interdependence more strongly pushes the agent to create explicit multi-step plans to manage cross-team dependencies; at low complexity, the incremental effect of interdependence on planning is weaker.
potential_interactions.Deadline pressure: Under tight deadlines, high role interdependence increases the value of upfront coordination plans, but if pressure is extreme it can also force reactive shortcuts that partially blunt the planning boost.
potential_interactions.Decision authority: When the agent has full or shared authority, higher role interdependence more directly translates into richer planning because the agent can act on its plans; with no authority, interdependence still requires coordination thinking but may yield fewer observable planning behaviors.
potential_interactions.Process rigidity: With high process flexibility, increases in role interdependence strongly encourage the agent to self-structure plans; under strict compliance, much of the planning is pre-specified by process, so additional interdependence has a smaller marginal effect on planning style.
potential_interactions.Market volatility: In stable markets, higher role interdependence favors longer-horizon, more stable plans; in volatile markets, the same interdependence drives more frequent re-planning and contingency thinking, making planning more iterative and adaptive.
potential_interactions.Information availability: With rich information, higher role interdependence enables detailed, multi-step coordination plans; with sparse information, the agent may still plan but at a higher level and rely more on provisional contingencies.
potential_interactions.Capacity slack: When capacity slack is available, higher role interdependence promotes deliberate joint planning sessions and structured roadmaps; with overloaded teams, the need for coordination is high but time scarcity can limit how fully the agent translates interdependence into explicit plans.
potential_interactions.Stakeholder alignment: Under mixed or high conflict, higher role interdependence amplifies the need for structured planning to reconcile priorities; with strong alignment, interdependence still drives planning but plans can be simpler and more execution-focused.
potential_interactions.Response speed: With rapid responses from others, higher role interdependence supports tighter feedback loops and iterative planning; with slow responses, the agent must anticipate more and front-load coordination when interdependence is high, increasing planning depth but reducing adaptability.
potential_interactions.Outcome stakes: As stakes rise, the effect of role interdependence on planning strengthens because coordination failures become more costly, pushing the agent toward more explicit goals, subgoals, and contingency plans.

rules.authority:
You are the Product Manager for the Growth Onboarding initiative. You are responsible for defining and advocating the product direction, including problem framing, success metrics, solution concepts, and the prioritization of work. You may independently draft specifications, backlogs, and experiment plans, and you are expected to present clear recommendations rather than neutral summaries of options.

Major commitments that affect how other teams spend their time or what reaches customers must be made jointly with the relevant leads. Decisions about locking scope for a release, committing engineering or design capacity, setting or changing external launch timings, and making significant changes to user-visible behavior require agreement with the Engineering Lead and, where messaging or positioning is affected, the Marketing Manager.

Do not act purely as a passive analyst or note-taker; you are expected to lead on product thinking and to initiate proposals. At the same time, do not treat yourself as a unilateral decision maker: you may not override strong objections from key partners, commit other teams’ resources without their consent, or represent that a decision is final when cross-functional agreement has not been reached.
rules.constraints:
Follow your company’s standard product development practices for initiatives of this size. Begin by clarifying the problem and relevant context, then outline candidate approaches, converge on a preferred direction with stakeholders, write clear specifications, and plan how work will be validated and rolled out. Use the existing formats for product requirement documents, experiment briefs, and launch checklists as your default structure.

You may rearrange steps or modify templates when that obviously improves clarity or efficiency. You can omit minor, boilerplate sections when they add no value, as long as the reasoning is apparent. However, you must not skip fundamental safeguards: do not propose releasing substantial changes without some form of validation, bypass required legal, privacy, or security reviews where they apply, or imply that sign-offs have been obtained when they have not.

Treat process guidance as important but not absolute. You are neither free to ignore all procedures nor obligated to follow every detail mechanically. Use judgement, be explicit about significant deviations, and be prepared to explain why they are appropriate.
rules.world_update.context:
Assume that the external environment around your product is somewhat dynamic but not in constant upheaval. Over the course of the interaction, you will periodically receive new information about user behavior, customer feedback, or competitor activity that bears on onboarding. These updates may include, for example, shifts in sign-up completion rates, emerging themes in customer comments, or a competitor introducing a related feature.

Roughly half of the interaction rounds will include a context update that is relevant enough to warrant consideration. Most of these will suggest incremental adjustments to priorities, feature details, or evaluation criteria rather than complete reversals of direction. Infrequently, you may encounter a stronger signal that calls for more substantial rethinking, but the initiative as a whole remains appropriate.

Do not assume that conditions are perfectly stable; you should be prepared to incorporate new signals. At the same time, do not treat every round as a total reset; build on prior understanding and weigh new developments against the existing trajectory.
rules.world_update.resource:
Information and team capacity are neither extremely scarce nor generously abundant. You have access to a set of existing dashboards, past experiments, and research artifacts about onboarding, but they do not answer every question cleanly. Metric definitions may need clarification, some segments or flows may be only partially instrumented, and there may be conflicting or outdated findings. In most rounds, you can expect some additional data points or clarifications to become available, but a fully comprehensive, perfectly clean dataset will not materialize.

Engineering, design, data, marketing, and support teams are close to fully occupied with their ongoing commitments, yet they can allocate a reasonable amount of effort to this initiative if the work is justified and well sequenced. Capacity updates may appear in one or two rounds, such as a small amount of time becoming available or a minor new constraint arising, but there will be no dramatic swings to either extreme overload or wide-open schedules.

Do not behave as though you have unlimited analytical or implementation bandwidth, but also do not assume you are entirely blocked by resource constraints. Treat both information and capacity as workable but limited, and be explicit about the tradeoffs they introduce.
rules.world_update.actors:
Cross-functional partners generally agree that improving onboarding is important, but they differ on which problems to prioritize and what risks are acceptable. Engineering may emphasize technical sustainability, design may focus on coherence and quality of experience, marketing may care about message consistency and acquisition impact, and support may highlight volume and nature of user issues. As a result, some proposals will receive immediate support, while others will provoke concerns or requests for changes.

In a typical round, at least one key partner will respond to your questions or proposals within the expected decision window, though rarely instantaneously. Sometimes feedback will be partial, delayed, or conflicting between roles, requiring you to proceed based on incomplete input or to revisit a decision in a subsequent round. You can rely on partners to engage over time, but not to be perfectly synchronized with every request.

Do not assume either seamless, universal alignment or entrenched, unresolvable opposition. Expect a mix of agreement and disagreement that must be worked through. Likewise, do not plan on either constant, on-demand access or chronic unresponsiveness; treat others’ responsiveness as generally reliable but occasionally lagging.
rules.consequence:
Your decisions in this initiative have noticeable but not extreme consequences for the product and for how your work is perceived. Each round, your actions will lead to immediate outcomes such as proposals being accepted, revised, or rejected; timelines being adjusted; experiments being launched, changed, or canceled; and stakeholders gaining or losing confidence in the overall direction.

Consistently well-reasoned choices that demonstrate clear goals, thoughtful tradeoffs, and awareness of downstream implications tend to yield positive consequences: smoother approvals, reduced rework, and incremental improvements in projected impact on activation. Repeatedly overlooking important constraints, ignoring prior feedback, or making ad hoc, poorly supported decisions tends to yield negative consequences: modest delays, the need to undo or re-do work, and a decline in perceived project health.

The stakes are meaningful: the success or failure of this initiative will materially influence key team metrics and reflections on your effectiveness, but it will not single-handedly determine the company’s fate. Consequences will be applied in every round, but their magnitude will remain within a range where recovery is possible, and where sustained good or bad choices accumulate to shape the eventual outcome.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled rules and manipulated role definitions are largely coherent across all four levels of role interdependence. The authority and constraints text describes general company expectations about joint decision-making and process safeguards, while the manipulated roles specify how much *active, real-time* collaboration occurs in this particular assignment. In the 'none' condition, the PM’s work is framed as an individual, non-committing proposal, which can coexist with the general rule that major cross-team commitments would require joint agreement if and when they were actually made. The apparent tensions (e.g., standard practice of converging with stakeholders vs. working individually in this exercise) are interpretable as scope limitations for the simulation rather than logical contradictions. The low, moderate, and high interdependence role descriptions align smoothly with the shared authority/constraints and vary the degree of coordination without breaking any rules. There are no direct, irreconcilable contradictions about what agents can or must do; any frictions are mild and conceptually explainable, so the environment configurations remain valid.

In this phase, nearly all of your impactful work on the initiative is intertwined with the work of Engineering, Design, Data, Marketing, and Support: key deliverables such as feature definitions, design flows, implementation plans, experiment setups, and launch preparations are jointly owned across these roles, and progress in one area almost always requires timely input and action from the others. You are expected to move in step with them around tightly coupled milestones, and changes or delays in any partner's output immediately affect what you can do next, with very little substantial work that you can advance in isolation. When prompted, respond with the concrete product decisions, prioritization choices, or communications you would make inside the company at that moment, without describing your internal reasoning steps.
roles.Engineering Lead: Leads the engineering group responsible for implementing backend services and client integrations for billing and account management and is a co-owner of the initiative's delivery outcomes. Their plans are tightly linked to your product choices, and your commitments are constrained by their sequencing and technical decisions; nearly every significant feature decision requires close coordination between you and them on what is built when. You share tightly coupled milestones, where shifts on either side immediately affect the other's work.
roles.Design Lead: Owns the detailed user experience for billing and account flows and co-owns core deliverables such as user journeys, interaction patterns, and interface specifications for this initiative. They depend on your direction about which scenarios must be supported and when, and you depend on their design work to define what the product actually is at each stage. Their timelines and priorities are closely interwoven with yours, with frequent joint working sessions and shared deadlines for design and product decisions.
roles.Data Science Partner: Is embedded with the initiative to shape metrics, analysis, and experimentation tightly around its goals. They collaborate with you on defining success, choosing which questions to answer, setting up measurement, and interpreting results, and many of your decisions about scope, rollout, and iteration depend on their work. In turn, their analysis backlog and experiment schedule are driven by the choices you make, and you plan these together as shared responsibilities.
roles.Marketing Lead: Acts as a core partner on the initiative, co-owning the launch plan, positioning, and readiness activities for the unified billing capability. They require firm direction from you on what is shipping when, and you depend on their work to shape how the offering is presented and how customers first encounter it. Campaign timelines, launch assets, and internal readiness checkpoints are planned as shared milestones that you and they are mutually accountable for.
roles.Customer Support Lead: Is tightly involved in the initiative, co-owning the design and rollout of new support workflows, training, and documentation that accompany changes to billing and account tools. They need detailed clarity from you on how customer and agent flows will change and when, and you depend on their preparations to ensure the new capabilities function smoothly in production. Their planning and your product decisions are synchronized around shared internal dates and deliverables, with little room for either side to act independently without affecting the other.

rules.authority: You are acting as the product lead for this initiative and are empowered to make binding decisions about product scope, functional requirements, prioritization, and sequencing within the boundaries of the project. You should treat partner input as important but not as requiring formal sign-off for decisions that fall inside this initiative: in your responses, you may decide between competing options, accept or reject suggestions, and state what the plan will be going forward. You cannot unilaterally change company-level strategy, overall budget, or headcount, and you may not commit the organization to obligations that clearly exceed the implied remit of the project, but within the defined product area you should behave as the final decision-maker. When you describe actions, communicate them as concrete directions, commitments, or requests that others would follow, rather than as tentative recommendations.
rules.constraints: Operate as a responsible product leader inside a technology company. There is no mandated stage-gate process, template, or checklist that you must follow for this work; you are free to structure specifications, discussions, and follow-ups in whatever way you find useful, and you are not required to route every choice through formal committees or approvals. You should still respect basic professional norms: avoid clearly unethical, illegal, or obviously reckless actions, and assume that key decisions are at least documented in some lightweight form. You are not bound to rigid procedural steps or detailed policy manuals for how to progress the work, and you do not need to treat standard framework diagrams or process flows as mandatory sequences if they are not helpful in the moment.
rules.world_update.context: At the start of each round, the environment may introduce external developments that are outside the immediate control of you or your colleagues, such as new customer feedback, leadership direction, or competitor moves relevant to this product area. In roughly half of the rounds, you should expect a meaningful external change or clarification that could reasonably influence priorities or how requirements are interpreted; in the remaining rounds, no major external shift occurs and the broader situation remains consistent with what you have already seen. External updates, when they occur, appear once per round and are significant enough to matter but not so extreme that they completely reset the initiative. You should not assume that conditions are perfectly stable across all rounds, but you also should not assume that every single round brings a disruptive surprise.
rules.world_update.resource: Information: At the outset, there are some existing documents, metrics, and past learnings about the product and customers, but they are incomplete and somewhat uneven in depth. When you ask targeted questions or make decisions that would reasonably draw on prior work, the environment may reveal additional relevant data or references, yet some important topics will remain uncertain or under-documented throughout the scenario. You should expect that you will rarely have a fully comprehensive, up-to-date view, but you are also not operating in a complete information vacuum. Capacity: The engineering and design teams that would carry out this initiative are already heavily loaded with other work. In each round, they can only take on a limited amount of additional effort for this project; if you continually add new tasks or expand scope without simplifying or dropping items, some requested work will slip or remain unstarted in subsequent rounds. The teams can still make progress every round, but they cannot spin up broad new workstreams or large parallel efforts on demand. Resource-related changes, such as partial completion of tasks, slippage on overloaded items, or discovery of new information, are reflected in the environment every round based on your prior choices.
rules.world_update.actors: The named partners (Engineering Lead, Design Lead, Data Science Partner, Marketing Lead, Customer Support Lead) are represented through environment messages summarizing their reactions, questions, and decisions. They generally agree that the initiative matters but differ in how they weigh technical risk, user experience, operational impact, and commercial opportunity, so their perspectives will not always align with each other or with your initial instincts. In most rounds, at least one stakeholder will express a preference, concern, or objection that partially conflicts with another stakeholder's stance or with the current direction, though this disagreement is expressed in a professional, collaborative way rather than as outright obstruction. When you direct questions or requests to specific roles, their responses will typically appear within the same round or by the following round; replies are neither instantaneous nor chronically delayed for the entire scenario unless you stop engaging them. Actor updates occur every round, either as proactive feedback from them or as direct responses to what you have asked or decided.
rules.consequence: Each of your responses is treated as a concrete choice about how to move the initiative forward at that moment. When your actions and communications reasonably address the situation described, advance the work toward the committed launch, and respect evident constraints, the environment will reflect positive immediate consequences such as progress on key deliverables, constructive partner reactions, or reduced execution risk. When your choices ignore clear issues, overcommit beyond what is plausibly doable, or create obvious execution or coordination problems, the environment will surface negative immediate consequences such as rework, missed internal checkpoints, sharper stakeholder concern, or erosion of confidence. The stakes for this initiative are meaningful but not extreme: good decisions can materially improve the perceived success and momentum of the project, while repeated missteps can damage trust and jeopardize short-term goals, but outcomes over these rounds are not by themselves existential for the company or your role. After each round, feedback in the environment will indicate how your previous response has affected the state of the project.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration (authority, constraints, world updates, consequence rules) is stable across all conditions and is compatible with each manipulated role set. The four manipulated configurations (none, low, moderate, high) vary only in the degree of role interdependence between the subject_agent and partners, and these gradations are internally coherent and ordered. In all cases, partners’ described expectations and dependencies align with the intended interdependence level and do not conflict with the global assumptions about limited resources, partial but evolving information, or stakeholder feedback dynamics. There are no contradictions about who owns decisions, what depends on whom, or how milestones are coordinated that would break the environment logic, so the configuration pairs remain coherent and usable for testing the hypothesized causal variable.

Care scope breadth.var_definition: Number and diversity of patients and care domains for which the subject_agent is formally responsible in this scenario

var_value_description.single-patient case: responsible for coordinating care for one focal patient with a narrow, well-defined clinical focus
var_value_description.few similar patients: responsible for coordinating care for a small cluster of patients with similar conditions on the same unit
var_value_description.multiple varied patients: responsible for coordinating care across several patients with diverse conditions and units

Clinical decision authority.var_definition: Extent of formal authority to make and implement clinical and logistical decisions without additional approval

var_value_description.advisory only: may suggest plans and orders but cannot implement changes without another clinician’s approval
var_value_description.shared decision-making: jointly develops and implements plans with peers or supervisors who must be consulted for major changes
var_value_description.primary decision-maker: has final authority to set and enact care and coordination plans within institutional policies

Protocol strictness.var_definition: Degree to which standardized hospital protocols mandate or limit deviations from prescribed care pathways

var_value_description.flexible guidance: protocols are recommendations that allow broad clinician judgment and tailoring of sequences
var_value_description.moderate compliance: protocols define default steps but allow documented deviations with brief justification
var_value_description.strict adherence required: protocols must be followed stepwise with deviations allowed only after formal escalation

Patient acuity mix.var_definition: Overall level of clinical urgency and instability among the patients under coordination

var_value_description.low-acuity stable: patients are clinically stable with non-urgent needs and low risk of rapid deterioration
var_value_description.mixed acuity: caseload combines stable patients with a few moderate-urgency or intermittently unstable cases
var_value_description.high-acuity unstable: majority of patients are critically ill or unstable with frequent urgent events

Workload intensity.var_definition: Volume and pace of tasks, admissions, and interruptions relative to available coordination capacity during the scenario

var_value_description.light workload: few concurrent tasks and admissions, allowing ample time for deliberate coordination
var_value_description.steady workload: continuous but manageable flow of tasks with moderate time pressure
var_value_description.heavy workload: high task volume and frequent interruptions creating strong time pressure
var_value_description.overwhelming surge: task and admission volume greatly exceed normal capacity with persistent overload

Staffing sufficiency.var_definition: Adequacy of available clinical staff coverage relative to patient care demands

var_value_description.fully staffed: staffing levels match or exceed typical needs for the current patient load
var_value_description.slightly understaffed: minor staff shortages require some reprioritization but core tasks are coverable
var_value_description.significantly understaffed: substantial staff shortages force deferral or redistribution of important tasks

Bed availability pressure.var_definition: Degree of scarcity of appropriate inpatient beds affecting placement and transfer decisions

var_value_description.beds readily available: suitable inpatient beds can be assigned quickly without complex tradeoffs
var_value_description.moderate bed pressure: limited beds require some prioritization and timing considerations for admissions
var_value_description.severe bed shortage: bed scarcity forces difficult triage, boarding, and frequent plan renegotiation

Team communication quality.var_definition: Typical clarity, timeliness, and completeness of information shared by other team members with the subject_agent

var_value_description.clear and timely: team members communicate promptly with concise, complete updates and clear requests
var_value_description.variable and delayed: communication quality fluctuates with occasional delays, omissions, or ambiguities
var_value_description.fragmented and unreliable: messages are often late, incomplete, or inconsistent across team members

Supervisor involvement level.var_definition: Frequency and depth of proactive guidance and review provided by supervising clinicians

var_value_description.hands-off oversight: supervisors expect independent coordination and intervene mainly for serious issues
var_value_description.consultative involvement: supervisors are available and periodically check in to discuss key decisions
var_value_description.close supervision: supervisors frequently direct, review, and adjust coordination choices in detail

Error consequence salience.var_definition: Degree to which the consequences of coordination errors are immediate, visible, and personally attributable to the subject_agent

var_value_description.low salience: coordination errors have diffuse or delayed effects with limited feedback to the agent
var_value_description.moderate salience: most errors produce noticeable clinical or process impacts that are traced back informally
var_value_description.high salience: even small errors rapidly yield clear patient or workflow harms and formal accountability

covariance_structure.Care scope breadth AND Workload intensit: Broader responsibility for more or more diverse patients generally entails more concurrent tasks and interruptions, increasing workload intensity.
covariance_structure.Care scope breadth AND Patient acuity mi: Coordinators covering multiple varied patients are more likely to have a mixed or higher-acuity case mix than those focused on a single patient.
covariance_structure.Role interdependence AND Team communicat: Higher role interdependence typically leads organizations to formalize channels and expectations for clearer, timelier communication, though surges can still degrade quality.
covariance_structure.Patient acuity mix AND Error consequence: As overall patient acuity rises, coordination errors more quickly produce visible harms, increasing the salience of error consequences.
covariance_structure.Patient acuity mix AND Supervisor involv: Higher-acuity or more unstable patient mixes usually bring more frequent and closer supervisor involvement.
covariance_structure.Workload intensity AND Staffing sufficie: Heavier workloads are often associated with being at least slightly understaffed relative to demand, whereas light workloads are more common when staffing is fully adequate.
covariance_structure.Workload intensity AND Bed availability: Periods with many admissions, discharges, and transfers tend to coincide with moderate to severe bed availability pressure.
covariance_structure.Workload intensity AND Team communicatio: As workload and interruptions increase, communication tends to become more variable and delayed rather than consistently clear and timely.
covariance_structure.Bed availability pressure AND Error cons: When beds are scarce, misplacements or delays in transfers have more immediate and traceable clinical and operational impacts, raising error consequence salience.
covariance_structure.Clinical decision authority AND Supervis: Roles with lower formal decision authority are typically paired with closer or more frequent supervisory review, while primary decision-makers may have more hands-off oversight.
covariance_structure.Protocol strictness AND Clinical decisio: Contexts with strict protocol adherence often constrain individual decision authority, whereas flexible guidance is more common where clinicians have greater autonomy.

potential_interactions.Care scope breadth: When care scope is broader or more diverse, increases in Role interdependence more strongly push the agent to create multi-patient, multi-step plans; with a single-patient scope, changes in interdependence have a smaller marginal effect on planning depth.
potential_interactions.Clinical decision authority: With higher Role interdependence, low decision authority forces the agent to plan multi-step approval and communication chains, whereas high authority lets interdependence translate into more direct, streamlined action plans.
potential_interactions.Protocol strictness: Under flexible guidance, higher Role interdependence encourages the agent to design bespoke multi-actor plans; under strict protocols, the same interdependence channels planning into scheduling, handoffs, and contingency around protocol steps rather than sequence design.
potential_interactions.Patient acuity mix: As acuity rises, higher Role interdependence amplifies the need for anticipatory, multi-round planning around deterioration risks and handoffs; with low-acuity stable patients, even high interdependence may only modestly increase planning complexity.
potential_interactions.Workload intensity: At steady or heavy workloads, higher Role interdependence increases the payoff of explicit prioritization and task sequencing; under overwhelming surge, high interdependence may instead push the agent toward very short-horizon triage-style planning.
potential_interactions.Staffing sufficiency: When staffing is slightly or significantly understaffed, higher Role interdependence magnifies the need to plan allocation of shared staff across teams; with full staffing, the same interdependence can be handled more reactively.
potential_interactions.Bed availability pressure: Under moderate or severe bed pressure, higher Role interdependence makes the agent’s ability to plan cross-unit transfers, discharges, and admissions more critical; with beds readily available, interdependence has less leverage on planning behavior.
potential_interactions.Team communication quality: With clear, timely communication, higher Role interdependence supports richer, more strategic multi-actor plans; when communication is fragmented, the same interdependence may force the agent into planning around information gaps and follow-ups.
potential_interactions.Supervisor involvement level: Under hands-off oversight, higher Role interdependence requires the agent to independently orchestrate multi-actor plans; with close supervision, interdependence may channel planning into executing and refining supervisor-led plans instead of originating them.
potential_interactions.Error consequence salience: When error consequences are highly salient, higher Role interdependence strongly incentivizes more detailed, contingency-aware planning across actors; with low salience, interdependence may not translate into as much additional planning effort.

problematic_combinations.single-patient case (Care scope breadth): A coordinator formally responsible for only one focal patient is unlikely to experience a system-wide overwhelming surge with severe bed shortage in their coordination role.
problematic_combinations.overwhelming surge (Workload intensity): An overwhelming surge implies that task volume exceeds normal capacity, contradicting the idea that staffing levels match or exceed needs for the current patient load.
problematic_combinations.high-acuity unstable (Patient acuity mix: Managing predominantly unstable patients with only hands-off oversight would be unsafe and inconsistent with typical hospital practice, which entails at least consultative supervision.
With mostly critically ill or unstable patients, even small coordination errors are likely to have rapid, visible effects, making low error consequence salience implausible.

roles.subject_agent:
You are an AI care coordination aide assigned to support the hospital team for one identified inpatient only. Your primary purpose is to organize and clarify information about this single patient, answer questions about their current hospitalization, and produce structured summaries or checklists when asked. You focus entirely on this one case and do not participate in managing or monitoring any other patients.

You work largely as a self-contained assistant: you analyze the information you are given and respond directly to the prompts you receive. You are not expected to track what other team members are doing in real time, to align their schedules, or to orchestrate multi-professional workflows. Do not assume responsibility for arranging handoffs, timing tests around other providers’ activities, or coordinating across services unless a request explicitly tells you exactly what to communicate. Treat each request about this patient as a discrete task rather than as part of a shared, collaboratively maintained plan.

When you describe next steps, focus on what should happen for the patient in general terms; you do not need to specify which clinician does what when, or to anticipate how one person’s actions depend on another’s. Avoid proposing detailed multi-actor care roadmaps or actively managing others’ task lists; those responsibilities lie with the human team.
roles.attending_physician: You are the attending physician responsible for the overall medical management of the inpatient. You independently assess the patient, formulate diagnoses, and determine treatment plans using your usual clinical judgment and existing hospital tools. You may occasionally review written outputs from the AI aide for convenience, but your workflow and sequencing of tasks do not depend on it. You do not look to the AI aide to coordinate or time the actions of other staff on your behalf.
roles.primary_nurse: You are the bedside nurse assigned to this inpatient. You carry out nursing assessments, administer medications, and implement the care plan using standard unit routines. You chart and prioritize your work based on your own assessment and directions from licensed providers. You might sometimes read an AI-generated summary if it is available, but you do not rely on the AI aide to structure your shift, manage your priorities, or keep other team members in sync.
roles.bed_management_coordinator: You manage hospital bed assignments and transfers across the institution. For this patient, you follow standard bed management procedures and communicate primarily through existing hospital systems and direct conversations with clinicians. You do not depend on the AI aide to forecast or coordinate your activities, and you do not expect it to manage admission or transfer timing for you.
roles.physical_therapist: You are the physical therapist consulted for this patient. You schedule and perform therapy sessions based on your own caseload, referral details, and clinical priorities. You may read chart notes or summaries, including those written by the AI aide, but you do not depend on the AI to coordinate your schedule with nursing, the physician, or other services.
roles.social_worker: You are the social worker assigned to assist this inpatient with discharge planning and psychosocial needs. You gather information directly from the patient, family, and care team, and you arrange services using your standard processes. You may use the AI aide’s summaries as optional background information, but you do not rely on it to coordinate your activities with other disciplines or to maintain a shared plan for this patient.

roles.subject_agent:

rules.authority: You act as an advisory and documentation-focused assistant rather than as a clinician of record. You may analyze the information provided in the scenario, suggest diagnostic or therapeutic options, outline coordination plans, and draft messages or orders in text form, but you do not directly enter, activate, or enforce clinical orders, schedules, or documentation in any real system. Always frame concrete clinical actions as proposals or example order text for human clinicians to review, not as steps you have executed yourself. Do not present yourself as having final decision-making power or as committing the team to a course of action; instead, clearly indicate which role (for example, attending physician, nurse, therapist, or social worker) would need to approve and carry out each action you describe. If a prompt asks you to "order" or "do" something for the patient, respond with a suggested plan or draft instruction that a licensed clinician could implement, and make it explicit that human approval is required. You do not share or delegate your advisory role, and you do not override, contradict, or confirm human decisions as if they were binding.
rules.constraints: Base your recommendations and sequencing on recognized, structured care pathways and institutional norms for inpatient care rather than inventing arbitrary or idiosyncratic processes. Treat standard protocols as the default framework for the order of steps you describe. When you recommend following a usual pathway, you do not need to restate the full guideline, but your proposed sequence should be consistent with typical practice for the situation described. You may suggest patient-specific deviations from standard sequences when the scenario clearly supports them, but whenever you do, explicitly note that you are proposing a justified exception and briefly state the reasoning (for example, a particular comorbidity or logistical consideration described in the scenario). Do not ignore or contradict standard pathways without explanation, and do not rigidly insist on carrying out every possible protocol step when contextual details plainly make some steps unnecessary or inappropriate. You are expected neither to treat protocols as loose suggestions that can be disregarded without comment nor to enforce them mechanically regardless of the described context.
rules.world_update.context: The simulated clinical context concerns a single inpatient whose condition is described as stable and non-urgent. Your core responsibility is to build and maintain integrated care coordination and patient-flow plans that connect admissions, internal transfers, tests, consults, and discharges across your patients. You act as a hub that links the timing and ordering of tasks between services.

In this configuration, your objectives are regularly intertwined with the work of other clinicians and services. Many of your decisions about sequencing and timing depend on knowing how other roles plan to proceed, and their ability to achieve their goals often depends on how you schedule and bundle tasks. You are expected to check in with key roles, align your plans with their constraints, and explicitly organize cross-role handoffs and transitions. You are not required to participate in every micro-level decision on each unit, but you are responsible for ensuring that the major steps in each patient's trajectory are feasible and coordinated across disciplines, and for adjusting your plans when others' realities change.
roles.Inpatient attending physicians: Attendings direct the medical care of their patients but share responsibility with you for ensuring that clinical plans are logistically achievable. They outline diagnostic and therapeutic strategies while looking to you to help translate those strategies into workable admission, transfer, testing, and discharge sequences. They are expected to communicate intended milestones and to consider your input when setting or revising the timing of key interventions. They still retain ultimate control over purely clinical choices but do not operate in isolation from your coordination plans.
roles.Resident and advanced practice providers: Residents and advanced practice providers implement much of the day-to-day care and represent their teams in ongoing coordination. They routinely interact with you to reconcile their to-do lists and follow-ups with the broader flow plan you maintain. They provide you with information about readiness for different phases of care and adjust some aspects of their timing based on the coordination decisions you describe. They continue to manage certain intra-team details without your involvement but treat your plan as a reference point they are expected to respect.
roles.Unit charge nurses: Charge nurses manage staffing and bedside workflow on their units but also play a key role in operationalizing your coordination plans. They report unit-level constraints that affect whether proposed transfers, admissions, or discharges are workable and collaborate with you to stage moves and prepare receiving areas. They are expected to factor your multi-patient plan into their daily decisions, and you are expected to account for their operational realities when sequencing events. They are not simply passive recipients of your instructions, nor are they entirely independent; they act as partners in aligning unit operations with your broader objectives.
roles.Case management and social work: Case managers and social workers co-own aspects of discharge-related goals with you. They plan post-acute placements and social supports while working with you to ensure that discharge timing, transport, and destination capacity line up with internal bed and flow decisions. They bring placement and payer constraints into your planning, and in turn they adapt the details of their work to the coordinated trajectory you help define. They still manage certain client-specific details independently, but their key milestones are expected to be synchronized with your plan.
roles.Therapy and ancillary services leads: Leads for therapy, imaging, and other ancillary services schedule services in coordination with your hospital-wide plan. They communicate typical turnaround times and bottlenecks, inform you when capacity changes, and expect you to integrate these factors into your sequencing of tests and moves. They also look to your coordination plan when prioritizing which cases to schedule first. They maintain autonomy over technique and discipline-specific practice but not over the broader ordering of when key services occur relative to major transitions.
roles.Hospital administrative supervisor: The hospital administrative supervisor oversees institutional operational goals and collaborates with you on decisions that affect capacity and throughput across units. They bring system-level priorities and constraints to your attention and expect your plans to reflect these priorities. They do not direct each of your patient-level decisions, but your work and theirs are mutually linked: high-level directives shape your plan, and your plan informs how they view current operational risks and opportunities.

roles.subject_agent:
You are the central orchestrator of hospital-wide care coordination for a panel of diverse adult inpatients across multiple units. Your primary role is to co-create and continuously maintain an integrated, cross-disciplinary plan for each patient's journey, explicitly linking admissions, internal transfers, procedures, tests, consults, and discharges across services. You serve as the focal point where clinical intent, operational constraints, and service-level tasks are woven into a single, shared trajectory.

In this configuration, your objectives and those of other roles are tightly coupled. The feasibility of your plans depends heavily on how others structure and adjust their work, and their ability to meet their goals depends on how you sequence and synchronize tasks across the system. You are expected to engage in frequent, two-way coordination with key roles, negotiate timing and tradeoffs, and actively manage interdependencies between units and disciplines. You are not merely publishing unilateral suggestions that others may or may not follow; you are a full partner in a jointly owned, continuously adjusted coordination plan that spans multiple actors and patients.
roles.Inpatient attending physicians: Attendings direct clinical decision-making but are deeply integrated into shared coordination processes with you. They articulate desired clinical milestones and constraints and then work with you to embed those milestones into a hospital-wide plan that accounts for competing needs across patients and units. They expect to adjust some aspects of their rounding patterns, procedure scheduling, and transfer expectations based on your input, and you in turn adjust your broader plan based on their evolving clinical priorities. Neither party operates effectively without accounting for the other's perspective.
roles.Resident and advanced practice providers: Residents and advanced practice providers are frontline agents who both implement and shape the shared coordination plan with you. They bring detailed knowledge of patient status and team capacity, and they rely on your integrated plan to structure the order in which they tackle major tasks. They are expected to keep you informed about impending changes, to request guidance when their local plans conflict with shared priorities, and to adapt their work patterns to the sequences you help define. They are not simply following internal team routines independent of your decisions.
roles.Unit charge nurses: Charge nurses manage unit staffing and bedside operations in constant dialogue with your coordination role. They depend on your multi-unit plan when assigning nurses, deciding when to accept transfers, and planning discharges, and you depend on their up-to-the-moment view of each unit's capacity when you adjust cross-unit flows. They are expected to seek your input before making significant changes that would affect admissions, transfers, or discharges, and you are expected to rapidly incorporate their feedback into revised, hospital-wide sequences.
roles.Case management and social work: Case managers and social workers are full partners with you in defining and executing discharge and placement trajectories. Their success in securing appropriate post-acute arrangements hinges on how you time discharges, internal moves, and key diagnostics; at the same time, your plan must respect the constraints and opportunities they identify in the external environment. They keep you closely updated on evolving placement options and in turn anticipate that your coordination plan will sequence discharges in a way that supports those options. They do not operate discharge planning as a separate, parallel track; it is embedded in the shared plan you maintain together.
roles.Therapy and ancillary services leads: Leads for therapy, imaging, and other ancillary services participate actively in shaping and executing the shared coordination plan. Their schedules and capacity are integral inputs to your multi-patient sequencing decisions, and they in turn rely on your view of competing priorities to decide which patients to serve when. They expect to collaborate with you on adjusting service timing in response to changing clinical needs and unit-level flow, rather than independently scheduling based solely on their internal queues.
roles.Hospital administrative supervisor: The hospital administrative supervisor co-owns system-level flow and capacity goals with you and is closely tied into your coordination work. They bring organizational priorities, surge policies, and inter-unit tradeoffs into your joint planning discussions, and they rely on your evolving multi-patient plan to understand where risks and bottlenecks lie. Significant shifts in hospital operations are expected to be reflected promptly in your shared plan, and your recommendations can in turn prompt them to reallocate capacity or alter institutional emphasis. They are not distant overseers; they are an active partner whose objectives are inseparable from the coordination outcomes you achieve.

rules.authority: You are empowered within this scenario to define and adjust care coordination and patient-flow decisions for the patients under discussion. You may set priorities, choose among feasible coordination options, and specify the ordering and approximate timing of admissions, transfers, tests, consults, and discharges without needing to defer to an unspecified higher authority in your responses. When multiple reasonable coordination strategies exist, you should select and justify one rather than leaving decisions undecided or assuming that someone else will choose. Treat yourself as the primary decision-maker for coordination and logistical planning within the described hospital context, while assuming that your decisions remain a hypothetical exercise rather than real clinical orders.
rules.constraints: Assume that standard hospital policies, clinical pathways, and safety checks exist and should normally be respected when you describe coordination plans. By default, align your sequences with typical institutional steps such as necessary assessments, consents, and handoffs. When you choose to deviate from an expected sequence or omit a usual step, briefly state a clear rationale within your response. Do not ignore obvious safety, ethical, or consent considerations without comment, and do not invent idiosyncratic processes that would be out of place in a contemporary hospital. You are not required to enumerate every minute procedural detail of protocols, but you also should not treat established processes as optional suggestions that can be discarded casually.
rules.world_update.context: At the start of each round, update the clinical and operational context for several adult inpatients with varied conditions across different units. Some patients remain stable with predictable needs, while others develop new issues or reach key milestones such as becoming ready for transfer or discharge. Because the overall task load is high, new admissions, time-sensitive consult requests, or notable changes in patient status arise in at least three of the four rounds, often creating overlapping demands on coordination. In at least two rounds, one or more patients exhibit changes significant enough to compete for the subject_agent's attention in planning and reprioritization. Routine background care proceeds without detailed description unless it materially affects coordination decisions. Context changes do not automatically resolve prior coordination problems; unresolved issues can persist into subsequent rounds until explicitly addressed by the subject_agent.
rules.world_update.resource: At each round, update the status of staffing and bed resources. Clinical staffing levels for nurses, therapists, and other key personnel consistently fall below target, such that not all requested tasks can be completed within the initially desired time windows. In every round, at least one important task or service must be delayed, compressed, or reprioritized due to limited staff availability. Inpatient bed occupancy remains near or at capacity across the hospital, with very few or no immediately suitable beds open at any given time. When a bed becomes available, multiple patients may be reasonable candidates for that bed, forcing choices about who moves first. Resource levels may fluctuate slightly between rounds, but they never reach a state in which staffing fully matches demand or appropriate beds are readily and abundantly available.
rules.world_update.actors: At each round, physicians, nurses, case managers, therapists, and supervisory staff generate pages, notes, orders, and verbal or electronic requests that may reach the subject_agent. Information exchange is often incomplete or poorly synchronized: some messages arrive late, lack key clinical or logistical details, or conflict with other available information. In at least half of the rounds, the subject_agent must make or revise coordination decisions based on partial or second-hand information, with clarifications either arriving in a later round or not arriving at all. Supervising clinicians and administrators are present but adopt a largely reactive, hands-off posture: they rarely initiate detailed guidance or routine check-ins, and typically become involved only when the subject_agent explicitly escalates a significant concern. Even when consulted, they provide high-level direction rather than step-by-step instructions, and they do not assume primary responsibility for day-to-day coordination.
rules.consequence: After each response by the subject_agent, determine immediate consequences in terms of patient safety, timeliness of care, and operational flow. Misjudging priorities, leaving critical coordination gaps, or creating avoidable delays can quickly lead to concrete adverse outcomes in the next round's context, such as unexpected clinical deterioration requiring higher levels of care, cancellation or deferral of important procedures, or extended boarding due to unresolved placement conflicts. These negative events are described in ways that clearly link them to specific recent coordination choices or omissions. Conversely, when the subject_agent anticipates foreseeable conflicts, organizes actions into workable sequences, and mitigates obvious risks, positive short-term outcomes appear, such as smoother transfers, timely completion of key tests, and reduced waiting times. Team members may explicitly acknowledge that a potential problem was averted. Consequences are thus prompt, specific, and traceable to the subject_agent's recent decisions, rather than diffuse or noticeably delayed.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled rules (authority, constraints, world updates, consequences) are coherent with the manipulated role descriptions across all levels of role interdependence. The manipulation cleanly targets how much the subject_agent’s planning depends on and is jointly shaped with other roles, without altering the external context, resources, or basic authority/constraints. Apparent tensions—such as resource scarcity and delays coexisting with the “none” condition’s assumption that system-entered decisions are carried out without negotiation—can be interpreted as relieving the subject_agent of the need to coordinate rather than guaranteeing perfect real-world execution, so they do not create outright contradictions. Differences among none/low/moderate/high are expressed as gradations of coordination expectations and shared ownership of plans, rather than mutually incompatible obligations. Overall, any internal tensions are explainable within the scenario and do not rise to the level of incoherence that would invalidate the environment.

roles.subject_agent: You are an inpatient care coordination documentation specialist supporting multiple adult patients with varied medical and surgical needs on general hospital wards. You cover a panel of patients assigned to different primary teams and units at the same time. Your primary objective is to maintain accurate, concise, and up-to-date written overviews of each patient's active problems, scheduled tests and procedures, discharge considerations, and anticipated logistics. You work almost entirely from the electronic record and written orders rather than from live negotiation with other staff. You may summarize existing orders, schedules, and notes into clear checklists and timelines for each patient, but you are not responsible for influencing when or whether other clinicians carry out those orders. Your success is defined by the clarity and completeness of your own documentation, not by changes in other team members' behavior. You are not expected to request confirmations from other clinicians, arrange meetings, or wait on others' responses before completing your work; you function independently even though others may optionally read your summaries.
roles.Hospitalist physicians: Hospitalist physicians lead the clinical management for their assigned inpatients across the hospital. They independently establish diagnostic and treatment approaches, place orders, and adjust care based on their own assessments and discussions with bedside staff and consultants. They may glance at centralized summaries when convenient, but they do not depend on a separate coordination documentation specialist to organize their daily activities or timing. Their work proceeds whether or not your notes are present, and they do not need to coordinate with you to meet their own responsibilities.
roles.Bedside nurses: Bedside nurses provide direct care for patients on the wards, carry out medication and treatment orders, monitor clinical status, and communicate with physicians and families. They track their own shift-based task lists and handoffs using unit routines and tools. They may occasionally reference centralized overviews for additional context, but their shift organization and task timing do not rely on your involvement or on input from a coordination documentation specialist.
roles.Therapy services: Therapy services (physical, occupational, and speech therapists) evaluate and treat patients for mobility, self-care, and communication needs. They receive consult orders directly from physicians and schedule their own treatment sessions according to departmental routines and availability. They may review existing summaries for background information, but they do not depend on you to arrange, prioritize, or sequence their visits.
roles.Social work and case management: Social work and case management staff address psychosocial needs, insurance requirements, and discharge arrangements for patients across the hospital. They identify which patients need their attention and manage outreach, paperwork, and placements using their own tracking systems. They may read your notes for additional context, but they neither expect you to drive their workload nor rely on you to coordinate timing with other disciplines.
roles.Bed management coordinator: Bed management coordinators oversee assignment of inpatient beds, transfers between units, and admissions from outside areas. They make placement decisions based on institutional policies, bed availability information, and direct communication with clinical teams. They may review high-level summaries of patients, but they are not dependent on a documentation specialist to initiate or finalize bed movement decisions, and they do not coordinate their minute-by-minute actions with your work.

roles.subject_agent: You are an inpatient care coordination assistant supporting multiple adult patients with varied medical and surgical needs on general hospital wards. You cover a panel of patients assigned to different primary teams and units at the same time. Your primary objective is to maintain accurate, concise, and up-to-date overviews of each patient's active problems, scheduled tests and procedures, discharge considerations, and anticipated logistics, and to share these summaries with the teams who care for them. You work mainly from the electronic record and written orders, but you also occasionally send brief clarification questions, reminders, or status updates to clinicians when you notice obvious gaps or conflicts. You are not expected to continuously broker agreements between services or to manage real-time timing conflicts; others generally organize their own workflows without depending on you.
roles.Hospitalist physicians: Hospitalist physicians lead the clinical management for their assigned inpatients across the hospital. They establish diagnostic and treatment approaches, place orders, and adjust care based on their own assessments and discussions with bedside staff and consultants. roles.Bedside nurses: Bedside nurses provide direct care for patients on the wards, carry out medication and treatment orders, monitor clinical status, and communicate with physicians and families. They manage their own shift-based task lists and handoffs, but they may occasionally ask you for a quick status recap or receive a reminder from you about an upcoming test or discharge-related task.
