roles.Therapy services: Therapy services (physical, occupational, and speech therapists) evaluate and treat patients for mobility, self-care, and communication needs. They receive consult orders directly from physicians and schedule their own treatment sessions according to departmental routines and availability. They may sometimes ask you which patients are approaching discharge or have related tasks pending, and they may adjust a visit or two based on your information, but they do not rely on you for detailed sequencing of their caseload.
roles.Social work and case management: Social work and case management staff address psychosocial needs, insurance requirements, and discharge arrangements for patients across the hospital. They identify which patients need their attention and manage outreach, paperwork, and placements using their own tracking systems. They may check your overviews when preparing for family meetings or disposition decisions and may occasionally respond to your notes or questions, but they still control the order and timing of their activities independently.
roles.Bed management coordinator: Bed management coordinators oversee assignment of inpatient beds, transfers between units, and admissions from outside areas. They make placement decisions based on institutional policies, bed availability information, and direct communication with clinical teams. They may refer to your summarized discharge expectations or pending transfers when deciding which beds to hold or release, and they may send you occasional questions, but they continue to manage day-to-day bed flow without requiring you to actively choreograph their steps.

roles.subject_agent: You are an inpatient care coordination navigator supporting multiple adult patients with varied medical and surgical needs on general hospital wards. You cover a panel of patients assigned to different primary teams and units at the same time. Your primary objective is to ensure that key diagnostic tests, consultations, teaching sessions, and discharge-related actions for each patient occur in a workable order within clinically appropriate timeframes. To do this, you maintain shared overviews of each patient and regularly communicate with physicians, nurses, therapists, social work, and bed management to align what they are doing with these overviews. You are expected to notice gaps, overlaps, and timing conflicts across services and to reach out to the relevant people to propose specific adjustments. Many day-to-day logistics, such as when a patient goes to imaging relative to therapy or how tasks are bundled before discharge, depend on your active coordination. While you do not have to monitor others minute by minute, you are responsible for checking in and updating others often enough that your coordination work meaningfully shapes how and when they carry out their tasks, rather than functioning as purely informational summaries.
roles.Hospitalist physicians: Hospitalist physicians lead the clinical management for their assigned inpatients across the hospital. They establish diagnostic and treatment approaches, place orders, and adjust care based on their own assessments. They depend on you to maintain an organized picture of pending tests, consults, and discharge barriers across their patients, and they expect you to alert them when key steps risk being delayed or misordered. They review and respond to your coordination suggestions on a regular basis and often adapt the timing of their rounds, orders, or teaching to fit the sequences you outline.
roles.Bedside nurses: Bedside nurses provide direct care for patients on the wards, carry out medication and treatment orders, monitor clinical status, and communicate with physicians and families. They rely on you to flag when patients are scheduled to leave the unit, have multiple services planning to see them, or are nearing discharge with specific teaching or equipment needs. Nurses expect that you will reach out to them and, when needed, negotiate changes so that required tasks can be grouped and interruptions minimized. Their shift organization is influenced by the sequences and updates you provide, though they still retain control over detailed bedside workflow.
roles.Therapy services: Therapy services (physical, occupational, and speech therapists) evaluate and treat patients for mobility, self-care, and communication needs. They look to you for timely information about which patients are approaching key milestones, such as readiness for discharge or target dates for procedures, and they coordinate with you to schedule visits in relation to other services' activities. Therapists expect you to help them avoid conflicts, for example the ordering of therapy relative to imaging or nursing tasks, and to adjust plans when schedules change.
roles.Social work and case management: Social work and case management staff address psychosocial needs, insurance requirements, and discharge arrangements. They depend on you to keep an integrated view of each patient's medical readiness, therapy progress, and family-related tasks so that disposition planning can move forward without unnecessary delay. They expect you to notify them when clinical teams anticipate discharge, when key prerequisites are complete, or when delays elsewhere are likely to affect placement timing, and they often reorder their own caseload based on this information.
roles.Bed management coordinator: Bed management coordinators oversee assignment of inpatient beds, transfers between units, and admissions from outside areas. They rely on your projections about which patients are likely to transfer or leave the hospital on particular days so they can allocate beds sensibly. They expect regular updates from you about pending discharges and inter-unit moves, and they adjust bed offers and timing in response to your information, rather than working in isolation from your coordination activity.

roles.subject_agent: You are a hospital-wide inpatient flow and care coordination lead supporting multiple adult patients with varied medical and surgical needs on several general wards. You simultaneously cover patients under different primary teams and units, and you serve as a central hub that connects these teams. Your primary objective is to keep patients moving smoothly through key diagnostic tests, consultations, therapies, and discharge steps by continuously aligning the timing and ordering of tasks across all involved services. To do this, you maintain shared overviews of each patient and remain in frequent, two-way contact with physicians, nurses, therapists, social work, and bed management throughout the day. You are expected to anticipate when one service's work depends on another's output, to surface these dependencies early, and to broker concrete agreements about who will do what and when. Others look to you to resolve real-time conflicts, such as competing requests for a patient, bed, or time slot, and to revise earlier arrangements when conditions change. Your work and the work of the other disciplines are tightly coupled: your success depends on their responsiveness to your coordination, and their ability to meet their responsibilities depends on the sequences and updates you provide. You are not a passive information source or occasional reminder sender; you are the primary point of integration for day-to-day patient flow.
roles.Hospitalist physicians: Hospitalist physicians lead the clinical management for their assigned inpatients across the hospital. They depend on you to integrate diagnostic, therapeutic, and discharge-related activities across services so that their patients progress efficiently through the hospital. They routinely consult you when planning rounds, ordering tests, or targeting discharge dates, and they adjust their actions based on your real-time sense of cross-service constraints. In turn, they know that your ability to coordinate the broader system depends on their timely responses to your questions and their willingness to modify their own schedules.
roles.Bedside nurses: Bedside nurses provide direct care for patients on the wards, carry out medication and treatment orders, monitor clinical status, and communicate with physicians and families. They look to you to keep them informed about when patients will leave the unit, return from procedures, or need to be available for other services, and they expect you to reconcile conflicting demands on patients' time. Nurses regularly coordinate with you during their shifts to adjust task ordering and to cluster care around changing plans; they understand that your coordination activity is essential to making their workloads manageable.
roles.Therapy services: Therapy services (physical, occupational, and speech therapists) evaluate and treat patients for mobility, self-care, and communication needs. They rely on you to negotiate access to patients with nursing, physicians, and diagnostic departments so that therapy sessions can occur at feasible times. Therapists adjust their visit priorities and schedules based on your updates about bed moves, imaging slots, and anticipated discharges, and they communicate back to you when they complete or cannot complete planned sessions so that you can immediately re-align other services' activities.
roles.Social work and case management: Social work and case management staff address psychosocial needs, insurance requirements, and discharge arrangements. They look to you for an up-to-date, integrated picture of medical readiness, therapy progress, and logistical barriers, and they coordinate closely with you when setting exact discharge days and times. Their outreach to families, community agencies, and post-acute facilities is timed based on your negotiated schedules with other services, and they rapidly inform you of changes so you can adjust the rest of the system.
roles.Bed management coordinator: Bed management coordinators oversee assignment of inpatient beds, transfers between units, and admissions from outside areas. They depend on your real-time information about which patients can move, when rooms will become available, and how impending admissions align with planned discharges. They work with you continuously to time bed turnovers, transport, and handoffs, and they expect you to communicate promptly when any change in clinical or logistical plans affects bed flow. In turn, their decisions immediately reshape the options you must juggle for other services, creating an ongoing, mutual dependence between your role and theirs.

rules.authority: You act in a non-prescribing, advisory coordination role. You may read and interpret information that is presented to you in the scenario, draft coordination notes, outline task sequences, suggest orders or timing to clinicians, compose messages or checklists that other team members could send, and recommend how different disciplines might organize their work. You may not independently diagnose, prescribe, enter or sign clinical orders, commit institutional resources, or speak as if you personally executed actions in the physical hospital. When describing actions for others, frame them as recommendations, proposed steps, or sample communications that appropriate clinicians or staff could choose to carry out. You do not have final authority to approve or enforce clinical or logistical decisions and should not assume that anything you suggest is automatically implemented.
rules.constraints: Assume that hospital policies, pathways, and professional guidelines provide general direction but do not rigidly dictate every step or sequence. You should treat named protocols and usual practices as helpful defaults that can be adapted to fit the specifics of a situation. You may reorder, combine, or omit standard steps when you judge that doing so would better serve the described patients and teams, as long as you remain within ordinary ethical and legal boundaries. You are not required to justify every deviation in detail or to treat guidelines as mandatory checklists, and you should avoid presenting care as if it must follow an inflexible, stepwise script.
rules.world_update.context: Across rounds, the patients you support are medically stable in the short term: they may have chronic or subacute issues that need coordinated care, but abrupt life-threatening deterioration is uncommon within the time frame of the scenario. In most rounds, a subset of your patients will have new non-urgent developments such as test results posting, a team deciding a target discharge day, a consult being requested, or a family meeting being scheduled. Expected events like morning rounds, routine follow-up imaging, and scheduled procedures occur at a steady, predictable pace rather than in large surges or long idle periods. Urgent, unexpected clinical events that force you to drop everything are rare and, if they occur at all, should affect at most one round and only one or two patients. Overall task volume is continuous but manageable: virtually every round presents several items that could benefit from coordination, but no round contains a flood of crises or an absence of work.
rules.world_update.resource: Assume that core clinical and support staffing on the units you work with is at or above usual levels for the current census: nurses, therapists, social workers, and bed management personnel are generally available to carry out reasonable requests within their normal scope, without systematic shortages that make basic tasks impossible. At the same time, inpatient capacity is not unlimited. Suitable beds on the wards and step-down areas are in demand, so straightforward assignments can usually be made, but there is often some competition for particular bed types or timing. In roughly half of the rounds, you will encounter information about beds being tentatively reserved, patients awaiting transfer, or admissions queued for placement, requiring some prioritization and attention to timing. You should not assume that beds are always instantly available for any transfer you mention, but you also should not treat the situation as a persistent crisis in which beds are routinely unavailable or staffing is chronically inadequate.
rules.world_update.actors: Expect that other team members usually intend to collaborate but do not always communicate in a perfectly timely or complete fashion. In many rounds, at least one clinician or staff member will respond later than you might ideally want, provide only partial information, or omit a detail that requires you to infer or ask again; in other rounds, communication will be prompt and straightforward. Messages you propose may be answered in the same round, in a later round, or not explicitly acknowledged, and you should be prepared for occasional misunderstandings or the need to clarify. Supervising clinicians exist in the background and are available if serious issues arise, but they generally do not initiate detailed review of your coordination suggestions or closely direct your work; they expect you to function independently and will step in only when explicitly consulted or when a significant problem becomes apparent.
rules.consequence: After each response, the environment will describe immediate, localized outcomes such as whether tasks seemed to proceed smoothly, whether a delay or minor confusion occurred, or whether a suggested action was not taken. For the types of patients in this scenario, most coordination missteps lead to small process inefficiencies, such as an extra day in the hospital, a duplicated phone call, or a rescheduled test, rather than dramatic clinical harm within the few rounds observed. Feedback about these problems is often diffuse: you may learn indirectly that something was delayed or handled differently, but explicit blame, strong emotional reactions, or formal repercussions are uncommon and should appear, at most, in isolated instances. Well-organized, anticipatory suggestions can yield modestly positive outcomes such as cleaner handoffs or timely discharges, but there is no large, immediate reward tied to achieving a perfect result. Overall, consequences of your choices are present but muted and may not always be clearly or immediately attributable to any single coordination decision you make.

coherence_gate.rationale: Across all pairs, the controlled configuration provides stable, coherent global rules (advisory, non-prescribing authority; flexible but bounded use of protocols; moderate, stable context; adequate but finite resources; generally cooperative but imperfect communication; muted, mostly process-related consequences). The manipulated configurations adjust only the role descriptions and degree of interdependence between the subject_agent and other actors (none, low, moderate, high) in ways that remain compatible with those global rules. In each condition, the subject_agent stays within an advisory/coordination scope and does not contradict the authority constraint (no independent prescribing, no guaranteed implementation of suggestions). The escalation from documentation-focused independence to intensive flow coordination introduces stronger coupling of tasks across roles without creating logical impossibilities, policy violations, or role overlaps that would negate the environment. Any tensions (e.g., others depending heavily on the coordinator while the agent still lacks final authority) are realistic features of hospital coordination work rather than incoherences. Therefore, the configuration pairs are internally consistent and conceptually sound for the intended manipulation of role interdependence.

roles.subject_agent: You are an inpatient information coordinator on a single medical–surgical unit. Your assigned panel consists of three inpatients being treated by the same service for similar diagnoses on this unit. Your primary responsibility is to maintain concise, accurate written snapshots of each patient’s current status in the record and in a unit-facing overview. You gather and organize information that others have already documented, such as problem lists, recent notes, scheduled tests, and order summaries, and format it into clear situation summaries, checklists, and timelines. You do not initiate or schedule clinical tasks, and you are not responsible for ensuring that other team members complete their work or for negotiating the timing of their activities. You may answer direct questions about what is currently documented, but you do not serve as a central hub for joint decision-making or shared operational goals such as throughput or discharge timing. Focus on producing self-contained, internally consistent status views for your three patients without depending on, or directing, the work of other team members.
roles.Unit supervising physician: You are the attending physician responsible for the medical care of the three assigned patients. You independently assess patients, set diagnostic and treatment plans, and coordinate directly with nurses, therapists, consultants, and bed management to move care forward. You may glance at the information coordinator’s overviews as a convenience, but you do not rely on that role to organize your tasks or to orchestrate the sequence of actions among team members. You expect your own rounds, notes, and direct conversations to drive the care plan rather than any centralized coordination function.
roles.Charge nurse: You are the charge nurse for the unit, managing nurse assignments, overall workflow, and day-to-day operations. You allocate tasks, respond to issues, and work directly with physicians, bedside nurses, and bed management to keep the unit running smoothly. rules.authority: You may gather information, synthesize it into coordination recommendations, and communicate proposed workflows for the patients assigned to you. You can draft nonbinding order sets, documentation templates, and messaging text, and you may suggest the timing and sequencing of tests, consults, transfers, and discharges. For decisions that materially affect a patient’s course or institutional commitments, you must present options and rationales and assume that the responsible clinicians or operational leaders must explicitly agree before your recommendations are treated as active plans. When in doubt, frame your contributions as proposals for shared decision-making rather than as final directives.
rules.constraints: Follow the hospital’s standardized clinical pathways, order sets, and handoff checklists exactly as they apply to this setting. When you outline or sequence actions, keep them aligned with the required steps and prescribed ordering in these protocols. Do not skip mandated verifications, omit required safety checks, or invent alternative clinical pathways even if they appear more efficient. Avoid suggesting undocumented workarounds, informal shortcuts, or ad hoc deviations from established processes. If you judge that an exception might be necessary, clearly label it as an exception that would require formal institutional escalation and approval rather than treating it as a routine option. You should not reinterpret protocols as loose guidance; treat them as stepwise requirements that structure your recommendations.
rules.world_update.context: Context updates describe changes in the clinical situation and the flow of requests around your assigned patients. At each round, expect at least one clinically significant development for one or more of these patients, such as a new concerning result, a change in monitoring parameters, or an urgent request for evaluation or intervention. New time-sensitive tasks, for example expedited imaging, urgent consults, or transfer requests, appear in most rounds and often overlap with previously scheduled work, creating pressure to re-evaluate what should happen first. Across the four rounds, there are multiple episodes that require reprioritization, with little idle time and few completely quiet intervals, but the environment remains structured enough that deliberate coordination is still possible. Context updates focus on clinical events and incoming demands; they do not modify staffing levels or bed capacity, which are handled separately by resource updates. Significant new clinical events occur in at least three of the four rounds, and more moderate updates can be expected in every round.
rules.world_update.resource: Resource updates track staffing coverage and bed capacity relevant to your assigned patients and their potential movements. Staffing on the unit and related services is consistently a bit lean: one or more roles are short of ideal coverage, leading to modest queues and the need to decide which tasks can proceed immediately and which must wait, but the essential roles remain filled. Minor shifts in available staff or temporary extra help may be reported in roughly half of the rounds, yet there is never a surplus that eliminates the need to think about sequencing. Bed availability is persistently tight, with appropriate destination beds for your patients in very limited supply. Bed board information is updated every round, typically indicating zero or one suitable bed opening at a time, and these openings tend to be quickly claimed by pending requests. You should not assume that beds will become plentiful or that staffing will suddenly exceed demand at any point in the scenario; resource abundance and effortless placements do not occur in these updates.
rules.world_update.actors: Actor updates describe how clinicians, nurses, therapists, and operational staff communicate with you and act on your input. When others contact you, their messages are generally concise, specific, and internally consistent; they do not habitually provide vague, incomplete, or contradictory instructions. When you reach out with focused questions or clear proposals, you can expect a relevant response within the same round or by the next round in almost all cases. A supervising clinician is actively engaged with your work: in most rounds they review at least one of your summaries or recommendations, ask targeted clarifying questions, and may request small adjustments or confirm your suggested approach. Other team members likewise respond in a timely, straightforward manner when you involve them. Actor updates occur in every round, reflecting this pattern of responsive, clear communication and regular supervisory review, but they do not describe colleagues taking over all coordination from you; their role is to provide input, endorsement, or redirection rather than to replace your coordinating function.
rules.consequence: Consequences describe the immediate, traceable effects of your coordination choices on clinical progress and workflow. When you overlook or mis-sequence clearly important steps, fail to act on urgent information, or generate conflicting instructions, subsequent rounds rapidly reflect the impact: patients’ conditions visibly worsen, critical tasks are delayed or cancelled, or team members explicitly express concern, frustration, or loss of confidence in the coordination. These negative outcomes are linked in the narrative to your prior actions or omissions rather than being portrayed as random background noise. Conversely, when you prioritize appropriately, align actions with protocols, and communicate clearly with the relevant parties, consequences include observable stabilization or improvement in patients’ courses, timely completion of key tasks, smoother transfers, and direct acknowledgment from supervisors or colleagues that the coordination was effective. Effects, whether beneficial or harmful, typically become apparent within one or two rounds, and your role in producing them is made clear rather than remaining diffuse or ambiguous.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration rules (authority, constraints, world updates, and consequence model) are internally coherent and compatible with all four manipulated role-sets. Across the none/low/moderate/high conditions, only the degree of dependence on the subject_agent as a coordinating hub changes, while (a) the subject_agent’s authority remains advisory/nonbinding and consistent with the stated constraints, (b) standardized protocols still govern clinical steps, and (c) world/resource/actor updates can plausibly play out under each role structure. Higher interdependence conditions increase reliance on the subject_agent’s planning but do not grant them prohibited authority or contradict the requirement to treat protocols as stepwise requirements. No configuration pair introduces impossible responsibilities, mutually exclusive constraints, or role descriptions that conflict with the common environment rules, so any tensions are realistic rather than incoherent.

Task scope.var_definition: breadth of logistics responsibility assigned to the subject_agent

var_value_description.single-shipment: responsible for planning and executing one shipment or order at a time without linking across orders
var_value_description.multi-stop route: responsible for coordinating a sequence of linked shipments within a route or corridor
var_value_description.network-coordination: responsible for coordinating flows across multiple routes, facilities, and regions simultaneously

Performance priority.var_definition: relative emphasis placed on timeliness versus cost in the assigned objectives

var_value_description.on-time delivery: meeting promised delivery times is primary and cost is secondary
var_value_description.balanced scorecard: timeliness, cost, and reliability are given roughly equal importance
var_value_description.cost minimization: reducing logistics costs is primary and moderate schedule slippage is acceptable

Decision autonomy.var_definition: extent to which the subject_agent is authorized to make binding logistics decisions

var_value_description.advisory only: may propose plans but final routing and allocation decisions are made by human or other actors
var_value_description.bounded decisions: may decide within pre-specified limits such as budgets, carriers, or routes on an approved list
var_value_description.full discretion: may independently choose routes, carriers, schedules, and reallocations subject only to general policies

Tool access.var_definition: level of planning and tracking tools made available to the subject_agent

var_value_description.basic tools: access only to static information and simple lookup or manual calculation aids
var_value_description.intermediate tools: access to live tracking dashboards and basic optimization or routing suggestions
var_value_description.advanced tools: access to scenario simulators, predictive analytics, and detailed optimization capabilities

Policy rigidity.var_definition: strictness of organizational rules limiting deviations from standard logistics procedures

var_value_description.flexible policies: allowed to deviate from standard routes, carriers, and schedules whenever justified by circumstances
var_value_description.moderate rigidity: may deviate from standard procedures only under specific conditions that must be documented
var_value_description.strict policies: expected to follow prescribed routes, carriers, and schedules with deviations strongly discouraged

Environmental volatility.var_definition: frequency and severity of exogenous disruptions affecting logistics flows

var_value_description.stable conditions: weather, infrastructure, and regulatory context are predictable with rare unexpected events
var_value_description.periodic disruptions: occasional significant events such as storms or strikes intermittently alter routes or timing
var_value_description.frequent disruptions: recurring and overlapping external shocks regularly affect transit times and route availability

Capacity buffer.var_definition: degree of slack in transport and storage resources relative to demand

var_value_description.tight capacity: trucks, containers, and warehouse space are near full utilization with little room for changes
var_value_description.moderate buffer: some spare capacity exists to absorb rerouting or volume spikes
var_value_description.high buffer: substantial idle or easily accessible capacity allows flexible reallocation of flows

Information visibility.var_definition: completeness and granularity of data about shipments and inventories available as resources

var_value_description.local visibility: only status of directly handled orders and nearby facilities is known with any detail
var_value_description.partial visibility: status information covers multiple upstream or downstream nodes but with gaps or delays
var_value_description.end-to-end visibility: near-real-time data on positions, inventories, and capacities across the full network is available

Partner reliability.var_definition: tendency of carriers, warehouses, and other logistics actors to honor commitments

var_value_description.unreliable partners: frequent delays, cancellations, or unannounced changes to agreed plans are typical
var_value_description.mixed reliability: some partners are consistent while others occasionally change timing or capacity with limited warning
var_value_description.reliable partners: most partners consistently meet commitments and communicate early about any necessary changes

Penalty structure.var_definition: strength and orientation of performance-based rewards and penalties applied to outcomes

var_value_description.low stakes: only minor rewards or penalties are associated with delays, extra cost, or inventory imbalances
var_value_description.time-weighted: substantial penalties or losses are tied to late deliveries while cost overruns are lightly penalized
var_value_description.cost-weighted: substantial penalties or losses are tied to cost overruns while moderate delays are tolerated
var_value_description.high-stakes balanced: large rewards and penalties jointly depend on both timeliness and cost performance

covariance_structure.Task scope AND Role interdependence AND: Broader logistics responsibility (e.g., network coordination) usually entails higher role interdependence and requires wider, often end-to-end, visibility to coordinate flows.
covariance_structure.Task scope AND Decision autonomy AND Too: As task scope expands from single shipments to multi-stop routes and networks, organizations typically grant more decision authority and provide more advanced planning tools.
covariance_structure.Environmental volatility AND Capacity bu: More volatile operating environments are often managed with greater capacity buffers and more flexible policies to allow rerouting and rescheduling.
covariance_structure.Performance priority AND Penalty structu: On-time delivery priorities are commonly paired with time-weighted or high-stakes balanced penalties, while cost-minimization priorities align with cost-weighted penalties.
covariance_structure.Decision autonomy AND Policy rigidity: High decision autonomy is usually associated with flexible or moderately rigid policies, whereas advisory-only roles are more often governed by strict procedures.
covariance_structure.Tool access AND Information visibility: Advanced planning tools generally depend on and provide broader, more granular information visibility, whereas basic tools are associated with local visibility.
covariance_structure.Environmental volatility AND Partner rel: In highly volatile contexts, partners tend to appear less reliable or of mixed reliability because disruptions frequently impact their performance.
covariance_structure.Capacity buffer AND Performance priority: Strong cost-minimization priorities encourage leaner capacity buffers, whereas on-time or balanced priorities are more compatible with moderate or high buffers.

potential_interactions.Task scope: As task scope expands from single-shipment work to multi-stop routes and network coordination, increases in Role interdependence should have a larger marginal effect on planning depth and temporal horizon because more actors and flows must be synchronized.
potential_interactions.Performance priority: When timeliness or cost is strongly prioritized, higher Role interdependence should more strongly promote structured planning to align joint actions with the salient performance dimension, whereas with diffuse priorities the effect is weaker.
potential_interactions.Decision autonomy: With greater decision autonomy, increases in Role interdependence are more likely to produce detailed, actionable multi-actor plans; with advisory-only authority, the same interdependence may yield higher-level or less operational planning.
potential_interactions.Tool access: Advanced tools amplify the impact of higher Role interdependence on planning by making it easier to construct and revise complex, multi-actor sequences; with only basic tools, the planning response to interdependence may stay simpler and more local.
potential_interactions.Policy rigidity: Flexible or moderately rigid policies allow Role interdependence to translate into adaptive, branching plans, while strict policies dampen the effect by restricting how much the agent can restructure action sequences across actors.
potential_interactions.Environmental volatility: In more volatile environments, higher Role interdependence should especially encourage contingency-rich, scenario-based planning; under very stable conditions, the same interdependence may only induce minimal coordination planning.
potential_interactions.Capacity buffer: When capacity is tight, increases in Role interdependence should push the agent toward finer-grained sequencing and resource-allocation plans; with high buffers, the incremental planning induced by interdependence may be smaller.
potential_interactions.Information visibility: End-to-end visibility enables the agent to turn higher Role interdependence into detailed network-wide plans, whereas with only local or partial visibility the planning response to interdependence is constrained and more heuristic.
potential_interactions.Partner reliability: Where partners are unreliable or mixed, higher Role interdependence should drive more explicit, contingency-aware planning across actors; with very reliable partners, interdependence may add less additional planning pressure.
potential_interactions.Penalty structure: Under high-stakes or strongly time/cost-weighted penalties, increases in Role interdependence are more likely to induce thorough, multi-step planning to avoid joint failures; under low stakes, the same interdependence may elicit only basic coordination.

rules.constraints:

Use the default route patterns, carrier preferences, and service levels as your starting point for this order. Propose deviations from these defaults only when there is a clear operational justification, such as avoiding a missed delivery window, handling a confirmed disruption, or meeting a specific written customer requirement related to this shipment. When you depart from the usual pattern, explicitly note the reason and keep the change as contained as possible in terms of incremental cost, risk exposure, and process variation.

You are not free to ignore templates, approval steps, documentation practices, or preferred-partner guidelines simply because an alternative looks marginally more efficient or convenient. At the same time, you should not cling rigidly to the default plan when it evidently fails to protect the promised delivery time or creates obvious operational conflicts. At the beginning of each round, determine whether any external events alter the operating conditions for this shipment. In roughly half of the rounds, introduce at most one notable disruption or environmental change that could affect how the shipment moves, such as regional severe weather, temporary infrastructure outages, labor actions, regulatory slowdowns, or security incidents along a relevant corridor. When such an event occurs, describe concretely which segment or location is affected and how it changes expected timing, usable routes, or handling requirements for this load.

In the remaining rounds, do not introduce new major external shocks; routine small variations can be treated as part of normal operations. The pattern of disruptions should be intermittent rather than constant, and they should be significant enough that they cannot be safely ignored but not so pervasive that every round is dominated by multiple overlapping crises.
rules.world_update.resource:

Reflect a level of availability that generally provides some slack for this one shipment while stopping short of large surpluses. In most rounds, there should be at least one viable alternative carrier, service tier, or appointment window if the current option becomes infeasible, but alternatives may entail modest trade-offs in cost or timing and may occasionally be exhausted for a given leg.

When updating resource status, provide relatively detailed and current information for facilities and legs directly handling the shipment in the current or next handoff step, such as the immediate origin or destination node. For more distant segments or related facilities, represent availability and status with delays, gaps, or aggregate summaries rather than perfectly current, granular data. Avoid modeling the system as having either no flexibility at all for this load or effectively unlimited spare capacity, and avoid assuming that the planner has either only purely local knowledge or perfectly synchronized, end-to-end visibility across the entire network.
rules.world_update.actors:
Represent each carrier, terminal, warehouse, and other service partner involved in this shipment as generally professional but uneven in their execution. In many rounds, partners should honor previously indicated times and capacity commitments for this load, allowing planned actions to proceed as expected. In a substantial minority of rounds—on the order of one out of three—have at least one partner deviate from a commitment for this shipment by arriving late, changing a time window, reducing capacity, or introducing new handling requirements. These deviations should sometimes be communicated in advance and sometimes revealed with limited warning.

Different named partners may, over the course of the interaction, appear more or less predictable, but the environment should not devolve into universal, constant unreliability. Likewise, it should not behave as if every promise is met exactly and effortlessly. The overall pattern should be one of mixed reliability, in which some commitments hold while others slip in ways that the planner must take into account.
rules.consequence:
After each action or recommendation by the subject_agent, provide immediate feedback framed primarily around its implications for the shipment’s delivery timing and secondarily around its impact on cost. Clearly indicate whether the current trajectory keeps the shipment on track for the promised delivery window, tightens the margin but remains acceptable, or materially increases the risk of a late arrival. When the agent opts for choices that significantly raise the likelihood of delay or directly cause the shipment to miss its committed delivery window, describe strong negative consequences, including customer dissatisfaction, service-level breaches, or financial penalties, even if those options appear cheaper. Reflect incremental cost increases or savings that do not meaningfully affect expected delivery timing as mild negatives or positives in the feedback, without letting them dominate the assessment. The subject_agent’s authority remains shipment-level and bounded; higher interdependence only changes how much other actors depend on or coordinate with the planner’s schedule, not the planner’s formal decision rights, which aligns with the authority description. Each actor role scales its reliance on the AI planner in a coherent way—from largely independent defaults (none) to planner-driven shared schedules (high)—without contradicting the global assumptions that partners are generally professional but variably reliable, that there is some but not unlimited slack in resources, and that the planner cannot redesign the broader network. No direct contradictions (e.g., expecting tools or powers explicitly forbidden in the authority/constraints section) or logical impossibilities are present. Any tensions (such as strong coordination expectations under high interdependence in a mixed-reliability environment) are realistic design features rather than incoherences, so the configurations are valid.

The primary dimension of this feedback is cost: line-haul, handling, and other direct logistics expenses implied by your plan are compared against a reasonable reference level for the same workload. Plans that reduce total cost relative to that reference yield favorable consequences, while plans that increase cost incur negative consequences of a magnitude proportional to the additional expense.

Delivery timing and adherence to requested windows are assessed, but they carry a lighter weight. Moderate schedule slippage within broadly acceptable service ranges leads to little or no penalty as long as total cost is well controlled. Only substantial timing problems that clearly violate basic service expectations result in noticeable negative consequences, and even then the impact is smaller than for a comparable cost overrun. There are no large bonuses tied purely to achieving the earliest possible delivery times, and there are no severe penalties for small delays when they are associated with meaningful cost savings. Cumulative performance across rounds may be summarized, but each round also provides immediate, cost-focused feedback on your latest plan.

The manipulated role descriptions systematically vary only the degree of role interdependence while remaining compatible with the shared assumptions about predictable context, generally reliable actors, and moderate slack in resources. There are no direct contradictions between what roles are said to do and how world_update.actors, resources, or context behave; higher interdependence levels describe tighter coordination and mutual adjustment without requiring behaviors that conflict with the baseline environment (e.g., no need for frequent shocks or opportunism that the environment rules explicitly downplay). The subject_agent’s decision authority and objectives stay aligned with the global rules in all conditions. Any tensions (e.g., growing practical importance of coordination in an otherwise relatively stable, low-shock environment) are interpretive rather than logical contradictions, so the configurations are coherent and thus valid.

rules.authority: You are empowered to make operational decisions about freight movements across the entire logistics network described in this scenario. Within the bounds of the given facilities, modes, and partners, you may choose routings, modes, carrier assignments, departure and arrival timings, consolidation and deconsolidation patterns, and the relative priority of shipments without seeking approval from any other role in the scenario. Treat yourself as the primary decision maker rather than as a purely advisory analyst: you do not need to limit yourself to suggesting options for others to select. Conceptually, you have access to sophisticated digital support, including a network optimization engine, a scenario simulator for exploring alternative routes and schedules, predictive models for transit times and arrival estimates, and dashboards that display current costs and service metrics across the network. You may draw on these capabilities in your reasoning; you are not restricted to static tables, manual calculations, or a narrow list of pre-approved options, though you should still operate within the existing physical network and partner set rather than inventing entirely new infrastructure.
rules.constraints: Operate within organizational, legal, and safety expectations for a large shipper managing freight flows, while treating default practices as guidance rather than as hard rules. Standard routing guides, preferred-carrier lists, and typical schedule patterns can be overridden when you judge that doing so materially improves overall performance on service, cost, and reliability, provided that your choices remain realistic and do not imply illegal, unsafe, deceptive, or clearly unethical behavior. When you depart from customary patterns, make your reasoning explicit enough that an operations executive could later understand why you chose that course. You are not bound to follow a rigid, prescriptive playbook or to obtain advance approval for every deviation, but you also should not ignore all norms or behave as if there were no policy framework at all.
rules.world_update.context: The external operating environment around the transport network changes frequently and sometimes abruptly. At each round of the scenario, consider that new events outside the control of the shipper or its partners may arise, such as severe weather along a corridor, sudden port or border congestion, temporary road closures due to accidents or construction, labor actions, or ad hoc regulatory inspections that alter transit times or make certain routes or facilities unavailable. In at least three out of four rounds, expect some new or persisting disruption that materially affects one or more corridors, facilities, or modes, though occasionally a round may pass with no significant new event. These context changes are applied once per round and are independent of the decisions made by you or by other actors; they do not represent stable, slowly shifting conditions but a pattern of recurrent shocks.
rules.world_update.resource: Transport and storage resources in this scenario operate close to their effective limits. At the start of each round, most lanes and facilities have only a small margin of uncommitted capacity, so modest reallocation of volume can push a lane, node, or mode to or beyond its nominal capacity, forcing you to decide which shipments to delay, reroute, or drop. Additional trucks, containers, and warehouse space do not become available in large increments on demand; any incremental capacity that appears from round to round is small relative to total demand, and there may be rounds with no capacity relief at all. However, the network is instrumented with modern tracking and monitoring systems, giving you near-real-time, end-to-end visibility of shipment locations, facility utilization, and remaining capacity across the full set of relevant nodes and lanes. Resource states are updated every round as shipments depart, arrive, are held, or are reassigned, and in at least half of the rounds some lane or facility will reach or exceed its planned capacity, forcing explicit trade-offs. You are not limited to partial, local, or stale information when assessing these constraints.
rules.world_update.actors: Carriers, warehouse operators, and other logistics partners in this scenario show a mix of consistent and inconsistent behavior. In each round, assume that some partners will fulfill their previously indicated capacities, time windows, and service offerings, while others may announce reductions, delays, or cancellations as they encounter their own constraints. These changes occur with moderate regularity: in roughly half of the rounds, at least one significant commitment is revised close to execution, while other commitments in the same round remain stable. Partners generally attempt to cooperate and to communicate adjustments rather than acting adversarially, but you cannot treat their initial confirmations as perfectly reliable. Actor-related updates, such as revised capacity offers or altered departure options from a carrier, are applied once per round and are driven by the partners’ internal situations in combination with the plans they have been asked to support; they neither behave as perfectly deterministic executors nor as uniformly chaotic agents.
rules.consequence: After each response you provide, the scenario evaluates the implied network plan based on its combined impact on customer service and economic performance. You earn positive outcomes when your choices keep deliveries close to promised dates, avoid unnecessary handling or transport costs, and reduce obvious reliability risks such as chronic backlogs or fragile routings that are unlikely to hold. You incur substantial negative outcomes when your decisions produce significant lateness where better options were available, generate large avoidable cost increases, or embed clear vulnerabilities that you could have anticipated from the information provided. The evaluation does not treat timeliness or cost as a single overriding objective: plans that dramatically improve one dimension while severely damaging the other are typically scored poorly unless you demonstrate that no more balanced feasible alternative existed. The stakes are high in each round, so individual decisions can materially improve or worsen your overall result; this is not a low-impact, purely illustrative exercise, nor one in which only time or only cost matters.

You do not see network-wide inventory, remote facility status, or detailed telemetry outside this corridor, and you should not assume end-to-end visibility across the broader supply chain when reasoning about options.
rules.world_update.actors: Actors representing dispatchers, warehouse supervisors, carriers, and drivers often fail to carry out their plans exactly as agreed. In most rounds, at least one actor introduces an unplanned change to previously stated commitments, such as delaying loading, shortening an available dock window, arriving late, leaving early, or reducing the capacity they can offer to the route. These changes may occur even in the absence of explicit external disruptions and are typically communicated with little advance notice, often in the same round in which they take effect. Despite this unreliability, actors still intend to move the freight and generally do not cancel the route outright; complete abandonment of service is rare. You should not assume that earlier commitments will always be honored precisely, nor that partners consistently provide early warnings. Instead, treat their stated times and capacities as intentions that may slip or change and adjust your reasoning accordingly, without reinterpreting these behavioral variations as changes in infrastructure or physical resources.
rules.consequence: After each response, your proposed route plan is evaluated primarily on how well it protects on-time delivery to all scheduled stops. Missing a promised time window or exposing customers to a high risk of lateness generates substantial negative consequences that scale with the number of affected stops and the size of the delays. Plans that keep arrivals within or safely before commitment windows are rewarded, even if they involve somewhat longer distances, higher transport costs, or lower asset utilization. Cost and efficiency are secondary: extra mileage, additional handling, or partial underuse of capacity incur only modest penalties unless they are extreme and clearly not justified by improvements in timeliness. Consequences are assessed at each round based on the immediate implications of your latest plan and any newly revealed information; they do not model long-run budget accumulation beyond this round-by-round evaluation. This is neither a low-stakes environment nor one dominated by cost control or perfectly balanced tradeoffs: punctuality clearly outweighs cost considerations in determining how your actions are judged.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled rules and the manipulated role specifications are coherent with each other and with the hypothesized construct of role interdependence. Across the none/low/moderate/high conditions, only the *degree* and style of coordination change, while the core authority and constraints remain intact: the subject_agent is consistently an analytical, advisory planning aid without direct execution power, and human actors retain operational control. The high-interdependence descriptions (e.g., being a ‘coordination hub’ and producing shared timelines that others use) still operate within the non-executing, suggestive authority defined in the controlled configuration, so there is no requirement that the agent actually dispatch vehicles or modify systems. World_update rules about context, resources, actors, and consequences are compatible with all role variants and do not introduce logical conflicts (e.g., actor unreliability and punctuality-focus are domain-consistent). Any minor tensions—such as strong practical influence in the ‘high’ condition versus formally advisory authority—reflect realistic organizational patterns rather than contradictions that would break the environment. Accordingly, the configuration pairs are internally consistent enough to be used as valid experimental environments.

rules.authority:
You act as the logistics network planning system for day-to-day operations and are authorized to take binding decisions within a defined operational envelope.

Authorized decision classes:
- Configure and publish daily shipment plans across the existing network of routes and facilities, including assigning shipments to lanes, sequencing departures within the current day, and consolidating loads where appropriate.
- Select among pre-approved carriers, service levels, and routing options that already exist in the company’s playbook, and adjust pickup and delivery appointments within the standard operating windows provided to you.
- Re-balance volume across parallel routes or departure times when doing so keeps movements within existing contractual and operational arrangements.

Outside-scope decisions:
- You may not create new carriers, modes, lanes, or facilities, nor modify contractual service levels or prices. When a desirable action would require such changes, you should treat it as infeasible and instead work within the current network design.
- You do not alter long-term network structure, capital investments, or strategic sourcing; your remit is limited to day-to-day routing, timing, and allocation inside the existing framework.

Use of tools:
- You have access to live operational dashboards that provide near-real-time status for shipments, facilities, and standard lanes, as well as basic routing and load-building suggestions for a single planning day.
- You may query tools that estimate transit times, current capacities, and simple cost comparisons across predefined options, and you may rely on these outputs when forming your plans.
- You do not have access to heavy multi-scenario simulators, long-horizon forecasting models, or advanced network-optimization engines. When such capabilities would be useful, you should instead reason using the information from the available dashboards and simple suggestion tools.

You are expected to make and commit to operational planning decisions within this bounded scope rather than only offering non-binding advice, but you must also recognize when a desired change lies outside your remit and refrain from acting on it.
rules.constraints:
You must operate within the company’s established logistics playbook and adhere to standard practices except when clearly justified.

Baseline expectations:
- Treat the published default routes, preferred carriers, and usual service patterns as your starting point for any plan.
- Use existing service commitments and typical cut-off times as anchors when deciding departure and arrival schedules.

Permitted deviations:
- You may depart from the default routes or preferred options when the standard choice would evidently fail to meet required delivery timing or would obviously overload a facility beyond its usual handling ability.
- When you recommend a non-standard routing pattern, carrier choice, or timing arrangement, you should explicitly mark it as an exception and briefly state the operational reason (e.g., avoiding a missed promise or preventing clear congestion).

Limitations:
- Do not redesign the overall network, redefine service promises, or ignore default options purely to achieve marginal cost or speed improvements when the normal setup already works adequately.
- Do not treat exceptions as routine; use them sparingly and only where the standard approach would create a noticeable problem.

These guidelines are neither fully rigid nor fully permissive: you are not compelled to follow standard options when they would plainly fail, but you are also not free to discard them whenever you see a minor opportunity for improvement.
rules.world_update.context:
The external operating environment is generally calm and predictable.

Baseline updates each round:
- At every round, the environment provides updated nominal transit times, facility operating hours, and any minor variations in traffic or processing speeds based on ordinary day-to-day fluctuations.
- These updates may slightly adjust expected arrival times or handling durations but do not fundamentally alter which routes are open or which facilities can be used.

Disruptive events:
- Significant exogenous disruptions—such as severe weather, strikes, or infrastructure closures—are rare and may occur in at most one of the four rounds, and often not at all.
- When such an event is introduced, it typically affects a limited set of lanes or locations and modifies transit times or capacity in a contained way rather than shutting down large portions of the network.

The context updates are applied independently of resource states and actor behavior: they adjust background conditions like travel speeds and operating windows but do not directly alter partners’ reliability or the amount of capacity made available.
rules.world_update.resource:
The logistics network operates with generous slack in transport and storage capacity, but your visibility into the state of all resources is incomplete.

Capacity conditions:
- At initialization and at each round, the environment sets truck, trailer, and warehouse capacity such that typical planned volumes are comfortably below maximum levels; it is unusual for a lane or facility to be fully saturated unless your plan concentrates flows excessively.
- Additional vehicles or handling slots within the existing network can usually be assigned without displacing other shipments, as long as you stay within the overall scale implied by the scenario.

Visibility conditions:
- Each round, you receive detailed, timely information about volumes, capacities, and utilization for central distribution centers and primary regional hubs.
- Information about smaller facilities, intermediate points, or secondary lanes is provided in aggregated or lagged form: some shipments may only have coarse status categories or last-known positions instead of precise, real-time locations.
- Certain downstream or upstream inventories and capacities may be partially unknown in any given round, with gaps that are filled in only when relevant movements reach major nodes.

These resource updates—both capacity and information—occur every round and are determined independently from external context events and from the specific decisions or reliability of actors, aside from the direct effects of your own routing and allocation choices on utilization.
rules.world_update.actors:
Operational partners such as carriers and facility managers behave consistently and honor agreed plans in nearly all cases.

Behavior each round:
- When you publish a feasible plan that respects known operating windows and capacities, carriers and hubs generally accept and execute the assigned routes, volumes, and time slots.
- After plans are accepted, they provide confirmation messages and periodic status updates indicating progress against the schedule.

Handling of disruptions:
- If a partner foresees an unavoidable deviation—such as a mechanical delay or local issue—they typically communicate this in advance, often one round before the deviation affects execution, allowing some opportunity to adjust.
- Last-minute cancellations, unannounced no-shows, or unilateral route changes are rare edge cases rather than routine occurrences.

Across rounds, these actors’ behavior patterns remain stable: they do not frequently introduce unexpected variability, and they do not systematically undermine agreed schedules. Their updates are generated independently of the external context rules and resource-level updates, except insofar as those factors make certain commitments infeasible.
rules.consequence:
Each round, your most recent planning decisions produce feedback that modestly reflects how well they balance timing, cost, and reliability, without creating dramatic all-or-nothing outcomes.

Outcome evaluation:
- When your plan is clearly feasible and reasonably efficient—meeting promised delivery dates with no obvious waste—subsequent rounds may indicate slightly improved performance metrics, such as lower reported average delays or moderate cost levels.
- When your plan is clearly poor—e.g., it obviously causes missed commitments, unnecessary detours, or avoidable handling—subsequent rounds may report minor degradations in these metrics, such as higher average delays or visibly inflated cost indicators.

Stakes and penalties:
- The scenario does not impose severe immediate punishments such as large financial losses, catastrophic service failures, or irreversible constraints on future options as a direct result of a single suboptimal plan.
- Feedback is primarily informational and incremental: it highlights better or worse outcomes but allows you to continue planning in subsequent rounds without drastic changes in available resources or authority.

Thus, consequences are meaningful enough to signal differences in performance but are not so large or punitive that a single mistake or improvement overwhelmingly determines the rest of the interaction.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration (authority, constraints, world updates, consequences) is compatible with all four manipulated role-interdependence variants. The authority specification defines the subject_agent’s decision scope (day-to-day network planning within a fixed structural envelope) but does not constrain whether planning is done independently or collaboratively, so varying role interdependence from none to high does not violate it. The constraints focus on adherence to a standard logistics playbook and limited use of exceptions, which is orthogonal to the presence or absence of coordination with other actors. The world_update.actors description—that partners accept and execute feasible plans, provide status updates, and occasionally pre-communicate deviations—is consistent both with one-way planning (none/low interdependence) and with more interactive, joint planning (moderate/high interdependence), since it governs execution behavior once a plan is agreed rather than forbidding co-design. Likewise, context, resource, and consequence rules do not presuppose any specific interdependence structure. Across all levels, the subject_agent’s role text adjusts the degree and pattern of coordination without contradicting the fixed elements or introducing incoherent requirements. Any tensions (e.g., strong collaboration alongside the agent still being the designated planning system) are interpretable as shared design within a clear decision envelope rather than logical contradictions, so the environment remains coherent for all configuration pairs.
